summary: Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan; the Spirit descends on Him like a dove, and the Father declares Him His beloved Son.
key_insight: Luke says Jesus was baptized “When all the people were baptized.” The sinless Son stood in line with people confessing their sins, and that is where the Father spoke His delight in Him.
story: While John was baptizing at the Jordan, Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee {Mk} to be baptized by him. Crowds of people had already been baptized. {Lk}

John tried to prevent Him, saying, “I need to be baptized by You, and are You coming to me?” Jesus answered, “Permit it to be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then John allowed Him. {Mt}

Jesus was baptized, and as He came up from the water and prayed, {Lk} He saw the heavens parting {Mk} and the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting upon Him. {Mt} The Holy Spirit came down in bodily form. {Lk}
A voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” {Mk}
differences: The voice says “This is My beloved Son” in Matthew and “You are My beloved Son” in Mark and Luke.
Only Matthew records John’s protest and Jesus’ answer about fulfilling all righteousness.
Luke alone says Jesus was praying and that the Spirit came “in bodily form”; Mark says the heavens were “parting.”
Mark alone names Nazareth as the town Jesus came from; Matthew says He came “from Galilee to John at the Jordan.”

fit.question: Matthew records the voice as “This is My beloved Son.” Mark and Luke have “You are My beloved Son.” Which did the Father say?

points.label: Words reported for their meaning
points.text: The Gospel writers often give the sense of what was said rather than a word-for-word record, just as they put Aramaic speech into Greek. All three agree on what the Father declared: Jesus is His beloved Son, and He delights in Him.

points.label: To Jesus, and about Him
points.text: Mark and Luke give the words as addressed to Jesus. Matthew gives them as a declaration to those standing by, the way John and others would carry the testimony away. McGarvey suggested this explanation.

fit.note: The Gospels report the Father’s words faithfully in meaning; Matthew turns them toward the hearers.
fit.short: Mark and Luke give the words as spoken to Jesus; Matthew gives them as testimony about Him. The meaning is the same.

scene.label: “To fulfill all righteousness”
scene.text: Jesus had no sins to confess. Most explanations fit together: He was doing everything God required, including answering God’s call through His prophet; He was standing with the sinful people He came to save; and He was stepping into His work as God’s Servant.

scene.label: The Jordan
scene.text: Israel crossed the Jordan into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). Tradition places Jesus’ baptism at a ford near Jericho, but the Gospels do not name the spot.

scene.label: Like a dove
scene.text: The Spirit came in a visible form like a dove; the Spirit did not become a bird. The prophets had said that the Spirit of the Lord would rest on the coming King and Servant (Isaiah 11:2; 61:1).

scene.label: The Father’s words
scene.text: They echo two Scriptures. In Psalm 2:7 God says to His anointed King, “You are My Son.” In Isaiah 42:1 He speaks of His Servant, “My Elect One in whom My soul delights! I have put My Spirit upon Him.” The royal Son and the Spirit-filled Servant are the same Person.

scene.label: About thirty
scene.text: Luke adds that Jesus was “about thirty years of age” when He began His ministry (Luke 3:23), the age at which Levites began their service at the tabernacle and David began to reign (Numbers 4:3; 2 Samuel 5:4).

witnesses.matthew: Alone records John’s protest and Jesus’ reply, answering the question every reader asks: why would the sinless One be baptized? In Matthew the voice speaks to all who stand by, “This is My beloved Son,” and the King is publicly named.
witnesses.mark: Tells it in three verses. Jesus sees the heavens “parting.” In Greek this is the same word Mark uses when the temple veil is torn at Jesus’ death (Mark 15:38), where a centurion says, “Truly this Man was the Son of God!” (15:39).
witnesses.luke: Notes that Jesus was praying, as Luke does at many turning points in Jesus’ life (6:12; 9:28–29; 22:41), and that the Spirit came in bodily form, something seen, not imagined.
witnesses.john: Does not record this event. John’s Gospel gives instead the Baptist’s later testimony that he saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove and remain on Jesus (John 1:32–34).

seeing.reveals: At the start of His ministry the Father speaks, the Spirit descends, and the Son stands in the water. Jesus is the beloved Son and the Spirit-anointed Servant who takes His place among sinners.
seeing.living: The Father declared His delight in Jesus before Jesus had preached a sermon or worked a miracle. Those who belong to Jesus are “accepted in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6), not on the strength of their performance. Serve God from that acceptance, not to earn it.
seeing.ponder: Do you serve God to win His pleasure, or from the pleasure He has already declared over His Son and over all who are in Him?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus stood with sinners, and heaven opened to declare Him the beloved Son.
outline: The sinless One comes to be baptized (13–14)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus’ first words in Matthew (3:15) use one of Matthew’s key words, “fulfill.” Matthew has been showing Scripture fulfilled since 1:22; now Jesus sets out to fulfill all that God requires, as He will say again: “I did not come to destroy but to fulfill” (5:17).
